slides.headline: אמא שלי,
slides.body:
את רואה איך אני נרגעת כשהוא בפה?
העיניים נסגרות, הגוף נהיה רך.

המוצץ שלי הוא לא סתם פלסטיק.
הוא איתי מאז שאני זוכרת את עצמי.
אז לפני שנפרדים ממנו,
יש לי כמה דברים **להגיד לך**.

scene.action: The girl lies on her bed with the pacifier, eyes half closed and body relaxed, her mother watching softly from the doorway.
scene.setting: A cosy Israeli child bedroom in the evening with a low wooden bed and a warm night light.

slides.body:
כשאני עייפה,
היד שלי מחפשת אותו לבד.
בין הכריות, מתחת לשמיכה.

הגוף שלי מבקש **להירגע**,
והוא מכיר רק דרך אחת.
אולי תני לי שמיכה רכה
או ארנב לחבק במקום?

scene.action: The sleepy girl searches under her pillow with one hand while hugging a soft plush rabbit with the other.
scene.setting: The same bedroom, pillows and a lilac blanket, soft lamp light.

slides.body:
ומול הטלוויזיה?
שם אני לא באמת צריכה אותו.
שם הוא **סתם הרגל**.

את יכולה להגיד לי
שהמוצץ נשאר רק במיטה.
אני כנראה אתווכח קצת. זה בסדר.

scene.action: The girl sits on the living room rug looking up at her mother, who kneels beside her and points gently toward the bedroom.
scene.setting: A warm Israeli living room with a low sofa and soft afternoon light.

slides.body:
רק דבר אחד, בבקשה:
אל תעלימי אותו **פתאום**.
אם אקום והוא לא יהיה, אני אבהל.

תגידי לי שלושה ימים לפני,
ותסמני איתי יום קבוע בלוח.

scene.action: The mother and the girl stand together at a family calendar on the kitchen wall, the girl drawing a big heart on one square.
scene.setting: A bright Israeli kitchen with a wooden table and a paper wall calendar.

slides.body:
את יודעת מה עוזר לי?
בגן יש ילדים גדולים,
ואף אחד מהם לא עם מוצץ.

כשאת אומרת לי
״גם את כבר גדולה, כמו הילדים בגן״,
אני מרגישה **קצת יותר גבוהה**.

scene.action: The girl stands on her tiptoes next to her mother, chin up and proud, while the mother smiles at her.
scene.setting: The hallway at home near the front door, a small backpack on a hook.

slides.body:
ואם אפשר,
אני רוצה לתת אותו **בעצמי**.
לתינוק קטן שצריך אותו.

הרבה דברים מחליטים בשבילי.
את זה אני רוצה להחליט לבד.

scene.action: The girl places her pacifier in a small decorated box with ribbons, her mother kneeling beside her.
scene.setting: The living room floor, a small gift box with colourful ribbons and flowers.

slides.body:
בלילות הראשונים יהיה לי קשה.
אני אתעורר בחושך
ואחפש אותו על השמיכה.

אז תבואי, תלטפי
ותגידי **״אני פה״**.
זה יעזור לי.

scene.action: In the dark bedroom the mother sits on the edge of the bed and strokes the girl's hair while she hugs her rabbit.
scene.setting: The same bedroom at night, only the warm night light glowing.

slides.body:
ואם תראי אותי
מכניסה אצבע לפה,
אל תיבהלי.

אני רק **מחפשת** דרך חדשה להירגע.
לאט לאט, לא הכל ביום אחד.

scene.action: The girl lies in bed with a finger near her mouth, her mother leaning in with a calm, kind look.
scene.setting: The same bedroom in the early evening, soft lamp light.

slides.body:
אני לא מפונקת, אמא. אני נפרדת.
מחבר שהרגיע אותי כל החיים שלי.

ואם אני מפחדת מדי,
תעצרי, ונחזור לזה אחר כך.

**אוהבת, רז**

sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health (with Oral Health Victoria), last reviewed 12 Jun 2026
sources.quote: Give your child the chance to stop their dummy habit when they are ready. ... Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four ... Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. ... Limit the use of the dummy to sleep or nighttime. ... Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. ... Give plenty of encouragement and keep it positive. ... The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Stopping gradually (not suddenly), limiting the dummy to sleep first, a chosen cuddly toy in its place, encouragement, and that the first few days are the hardest. Most children stop between 2 and 4. An Australian state health service page, applied to Israeli families as general child-health advice.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library (no date shown)
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. ... Once they are using their dummy less, set a date for being ‘dummy free’. ... Make sure you and other caregivers remove any bottles and dummies from your child’s sight. ... Using distraction techniques can help when asked for bottles or dummies.
sources.supports: Limit the dummy to naps and bedtime first, set a dummy-free date once use is down, keep it out of sight, and distract when the child asks. NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Stopping use of a dummy and/or bottle
sources.publisher: Derbyshire Family Health Service (Derbyshire Community Health Services NHS Foundation Trust, no date shown)
sources.quote: reducing the amount a dummy is used over the day is a good way to start the transition. ... Help them learn new ways to soothe themselves, such as using a favourite blanket or toy instead of the dummy. ... Try sending the dummy away to Santa, the Easter Bunny, the Tooth Fairy or the Dummy Fairy. ... Exchange the dummy or bottle for a toy or activity or new toothbrush. ... Praise times without the dummy, keep it out of sight and reach, set clear rules and stick to them. ... all parents and carers (including childcare settings) should follow the same steps ... Keep the dummy in the bedroom (if possible), try to remove the dummy once they are asleep.
sources.supports: Cut down the dummy over the day, teach a new way to soothe, a dummy fairy or a swap for a toy, praise dummy-free times, keep it out of sight, the same rules for every carer, and take it out once the child is asleep. NHS trust webpage for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Pacifier Weaning: When Is It the Right Time?
sources.publisher: Healthline (written by Rhona Lewis, medically reviewed by Karen Gill, M.D., 28 Aug 2020)
sources.quote: Explain to your toddler that in 3 days' time, you'll be taking away their paci ... On the day of reckoning, remove all pacifiers. ... Show your child that they can manage without their paci by gently stretching out the time ... Best practice is to offer your toddler another comfort toy like a teddy, blanket, whistle, or teether. ... When they successfully go without the paci, praise them loudly. ... Within 2 days, the crying spells will likely be behind you.
sources.supports: Tell the child in advance, a quick route (3 days notice, then all pacifiers go) and a slow route (stretch the time), a comfort toy in its place, loud praise, and that for the quick route the crying spells are likely over within 2 days. A medically reviewed consumer page, not a clinical guideline.

sources.title: How to Help Your Child Develop Empathy
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (page dated 1 Feb 2016)
sources.quote: Read stories about feelings.
sources.supports: Reading stories about feelings is one of the ways Zero To Three suggests to help a child with big feelings. The page is about empathy, not about pacifiers; used only as support for reading stories about a hard moment.

sources.title: Dummies
sources.publisher: Better Health Channel, Victorian Department of Health (with Oral Health Victoria), last reviewed 12 Jun 2026
sources.quote: Give your child the chance to stop their dummy habit when they are ready. ... Most children stop sucking habits between the ages of two and four ... Avoid trying to stop dummy use suddenly, as it can lead to other oral habits such as thumb or finger sucking. ... Limit the use of the dummy to sleep or nighttime. ... Consider replacing it with a toy, maybe a cuddly toy they have chosen and can hold when they would be using the dummy. ... Give plenty of encouragement and keep it positive. ... The first few days without a dummy are likely to be the most difficult.
sources.supports: Stopping gradually (not suddenly), limiting the dummy to sleep first, a chosen cuddly toy in its place, encouragement, and that the first few days are the hardest. Most children stop between 2 and 4. An Australian state health service page, applied to Israeli families as general child-health advice.

sources.title: Weaning off dummies and bottles
sources.publisher: Sheffield Children's NHS Foundation Trust, Resource Library (no date shown)
sources.quote: Start by just letting your child use their dummy for nap times and bed time. ... Once they are using their dummy less, set a date for being ‘dummy free’. ... Make sure you and other caregivers remove any bottles and dummies from your child’s sight. ... Using distraction techniques can help when asked for bottles or dummies.
sources.supports: Limit the dummy to naps and bedtime first, set a dummy-free date once use is down, keep it out of sight, and distract when the child asks. NHS trust leaflet for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Stopping use of a dummy and/or bottle
sources.publisher: Derbyshire Family Health Service (Derbyshire Community Health Services NHS Foundation Trust, no date shown)
sources.quote: reducing the amount a dummy is used over the day is a good way to start the transition. ... Help them learn new ways to soothe themselves, such as using a favourite blanket or toy instead of the dummy. ... Try sending the dummy away to Santa, the Easter Bunny, the Tooth Fairy or the Dummy Fairy. ... Exchange the dummy or bottle for a toy or activity or new toothbrush. ... Praise times without the dummy, keep it out of sight and reach, set clear rules and stick to them. ... all parents and carers (including childcare settings) should follow the same steps ... Keep the dummy in the bedroom (if possible), try to remove the dummy once they are asleep.
sources.supports: Cut down the dummy over the day, teach a new way to soothe, a dummy fairy or a swap for a toy, praise dummy-free times, keep it out of sight, the same rules for every carer, and take it out once the child is asleep. NHS trust webpage for UK families, used as general advice.

sources.title: Pacifier Weaning: When Is It the Right Time?
sources.publisher: Healthline (written by Rhona Lewis, medically reviewed by Karen Gill, M.D., 28 Aug 2020)
sources.quote: Explain to your toddler that in 3 days' time, you'll be taking away their paci ... On the day of reckoning, remove all pacifiers. ... Show your child that they can manage without their paci by gently stretching out the time ... Best practice is to offer your toddler another comfort toy like a teddy, blanket, whistle, or teether. ... When they successfully go without the paci, praise them loudly. ... Within 2 days, the crying spells will likely be behind you.
sources.supports: Tell the child in advance, a quick route (3 days notice, then all pacifiers go) and a slow route (stretch the time), a comfort toy in its place, loud praise, and that for the quick route the crying spells are likely over within 2 days. A medically reviewed consumer page, not a clinical guideline.

post_text.fb_text:
אני יודע שהגיע הזמן 🧸
ראיתי איך את מסתכלת על המוצץ,
ושמעתי אותך מדברת על זה בטלפון.
אני לא מתנגד, באמת.
אני רק צריך שנעשה את זה ביחד,
ושתדעי מה עוזר לי.

תספרי לי לפני שזה קורה
אם אקום והמוצץ לא שם, בלי הסבר,
אני אחפש אותו כל היום.
אבל אם תגידי לי כמה ימים לפני,
יהיה לי זמן להתכונן.
אפילו להיפרד ממנו יפה.

המוצץ נשאר במיטה
מה את רואה:
אני מבקש מוצץ מול הטלוויזיה.
מה קורה לי בפנים:
אני משועמם, לא עייף.
אם הוא נשאר רק במיטה,
אני לומד שביום אפשר בלעדיו.

דובי שאני בוחר לבד
לא סתם דובי.
אחד שאני בוחר.
רך, קטן, שלי.
שאחבק במקום המוצץ.

תגידי לי שאני גדול?
כשאני מתעורר בלי מוצץ,
אני מחכה לראות את הפנים שלך.
אם את מחייכת ואומרת לי
״אביב, ישנת כמו גדול!״
אני מרגיש גבוה כל היום.

ואם אבקש אותו שוב בלילה
זה יקרה, כנראה בלילות הראשונים.
אל תכעסי, ואל תחזירי אותו.
חבקי אותי, תני לי את הדובי,
ותזכירי לי בשקט שהוא כבר נפרד מאיתנו.

אני לא מתעקש סתם, אמא
המוצץ היה איתי מאז שנולדתי.
אני צריך קצת זמן להיפרד ממנו.
ועם הדברים האלה,
אני יודע שאני מצליח.

תשמרי את הפוסט
לפעם הבאה שהוא מחפש את המוצץ 🔖

sources.title: Potty Training Regression
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: Your first response when this happens should be to have them examined by their pediatrician to be sure the cause is not physical. Regression sometimes signals an infection or other disorder that requires medical treatment. If medical causes have been ruled out, however, your child is probably just responding in the only way they know how to a recent change in their environment or some other source of stress in their life. ... Change in the child-care routine ... The mother's pregnancy or the birth of a new sibling ... An upcoming or recent move to a new home ... Constipation/painful bowel movements ... Urinary tract infection ... Upsetting as regression can be to parents, it usually doesn't last very long. In many cases, the child picks up where she left off in toilet training after a few days or weeks.
sources.supports: Toilet training regression: see the pediatrician first to rule out physical causes such as constipation or a urinary tract infection; otherwise it is usually a response to a change or stress (new child care, new sibling, a move); it usually lasts days or weeks. Tips on the same page: ask the child why, fix what can be fixed (familiar objects around the potty, going with the child to the child-care bathroom), ask the child for ideas so they own the solution, be clear and confident about expectations with hugs, praise and stickers, and consider a break only if regression stretches on for a month or more.

sources.title: Emotional Issues and Potty Training Problems
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: At about three years of age, children start developing the capacity to experience discomfort, or shame, when they have done something they know is wrong. ... A child who longs for their parents' approval may suddenly start to feel embarrassed or ashamed after a bathroom accident, no matter how accepting their parents are actually likely to be. ... There is no cause to criticize or punish a child who behaves in this way. ... The best response when you find your child hiding their accidents from you is to gently tell them that you know they had an accident, that it's okay, and that you know they will do better next time. Then ask them to help you clean up ... If they feel you have been too controlling about bathroom use—constantly asking if they need to go instead of letting them direct their own behavior—they may resist going until it's too late and they have an accident instead. A more active imagination and a tendency toward magical thinking may cause them to fear the toilet and start to avoid it. ... try to avoid major concessions such as returning to diapers. Instead, consider offering to put them in training pants under their underwear for a while, put the potty in their room, accompany them to the preschool bathroom before the school day begins, or otherwise compromise until they feel more secure.
sources.supports: From about age 3 children can feel shame after an accident and may hide it; no criticism or punishment; say gently that it is okay and they will do better next time, then ask them to help clean up; constantly asking whether they need to go can backfire; fear of the toilet is possible; avoid going back to diapers, offer training pants, the potty in their room or going with them to the preschool bathroom.

sources.title: Potty Training
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (medically reviewed by KidsHealth Medical Experts, date reviewed March 2019)
sources.quote: Avoid clothes that are hard to take off, such as overalls and shirts that snap in the crotch. Kids who are potty training need to be able to undress themselves. ... Offer your child small rewards, such as stickers or time reading, every time your child goes in the potty. ... Make sure all caregivers — including babysitters, grandparents, and daycare workers — follow the same routine ... Praise all attempts to use the toilet, even if nothing happens. And remember that accidents will happen. It's important not to punish potty-training children or show disappointment when they wet or soil themselves or the bed. Instead, tell your child that it was an accident and offer your support. ... Many kids who've been using the potty have some trouble during times of stress. For example, a 2- or 3-year-old dealing with a new sibling may start having accidents.
sources.supports: Do not punish or show disappointment after an accident; tell the child it was an accident and offer support; praise attempts; stickers; clothes the child can take off alone; all caregivers use the same routine; stress such as a new sibling can bring accidents back.

claims.supports: AAP: gently tell them it's okay and that they will do better next time; shame from about age 3.
AAP: regression is usually a response to a change or stress; ask the child why.

sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: Your first response when this happens should be to have them examined by their pediatrician to be sure the cause is not physical. sources.supports: Toilet training regression: see the pediatrician first to rule out physical causes such as constipation or a urinary tract infection; otherwise it is usually a response to a change or stress (new child care, new sibling, a move); it usually lasts days or weeks. Tips on the same page: ask the child why, fix what can be fixed (familiar objects around the potty, going with the child to the child-care bathroom), ask the child for ideas so they own the solution, be clear and confident about expectations with hugs, praise and stickers, and consider a break only if regression stretches on for a month or more.

sources.title: Emotional Issues and Potty Training Problems
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (last updated 25 May 2022; adapted from the AAP Guide to Toilet Training, 2nd Edition)
sources.quote: At about three years of age, children start developing the capacity to experience discomfort, or shame, when they have done something they know is wrong. ... A child who longs for their parents' approval may suddenly start to feel embarrassed or ashamed after a bathroom accident, no matter how accepting their parents are actually likely to be. ... There is no cause to criticize or punish a child who behaves in this way. ... The best response when you find your child hiding their accidents from you is to gently tell them that you know they had an accident, that it's okay, and that you know they will do better next time. Then ask them to help you clean up ... If they feel you have been too controlling about bathroom use—constantly asking if they need to go instead of letting them direct their own behavior—they may resist going until it's too late and they have an accident instead. A more active imagination and a tendency toward magical thinking may cause them to fear the toilet and start to avoid it. ... try to avoid major concessions such as returning to diapers. Instead, consider offering to put them in training pants under their underwear for a while, put the potty in their room, accompany them to the preschool bathroom before the school day begins, or otherwise compromise until they feel more secure.

post_text.fb_text:
פעם הלכתי לשירותים לבד 🏠
אמרתי ״אני צריכה״ ורצתי.
הורדתי לבד, שטפתי ידיים לבד,
ואת מחאת לי כפיים מהמסדרון.
הייתי גאה בעצמי.

ופעם הלילות היו שקטים
קמתי יבשה, בבוקר רצתי אלייך,
והראיתי לך את המיטה.
סיפרת לסבתא בטלפון,
ואני שמעתי וחייכתי מאוזן לאוזן.

ואז עברנו דירה
ארגזים בכל מקום, חדר חדש,
שירותים בצד השני של המסדרון.
בלילה הראשון לא מצאתי את הדלת,
וכל הקירות נראו לי זרים.

אני שוב מפספסת
בסלון, באמצע משחק, בלי לשים לב.
את מסתכלת עליי, ואני מסתכלת על הרצפה.
מה יעזור לי:
לשמוע ״זה פספוס, זה קורה״,
בלי פנים מאוכזבות.

אני מסתירה תחתונים רטובים
מתחת למיטה, מאחורי הארון.
לא כדי לשקר לך.
אני פשוט מתביישת.
מה יעזור לי:
שתגידי שזה בסדר,
ונכבס אותם ביחד.

אני מפחדת מהשירותים החדשים
הם רחוקים, והאור שם חזק ולבן.
האסלה גדולה, והרגליים שלי באוויר.
מה יעזור לי:
להביא איתנו את השרפרף הישן,
והמגבת שלי עם הפילים.

הסיר הישן חוזר לחדר שלי
קרוב, מוכר, בלי מסדרון ארוך.
ואת שואלת אותי:
״מה יעזור לך, תמר?״
אני בוחרת מדבקה לכל ניסיון,
ומרגישה שוב גדולה.

זה לא דווקא, אמא
הכל השתנה סביבי בבת אחת.
הגוף שלי צריך קצת זמן להתרגל.
וכשאני מרגישה שוב בבית,
אני חוזרת להיות הגדולה שלך.

תשמרי את הפוסט
לפעם הבאה שהיא מפספסת 🔖
